AST-Coathanger.why: A bright, unmistakable upside-down coathanger of ten 5th-7th mag stars that fits the field perfectly; one of the most-loved binocular sights.

AST-DavisDog.why: A big 3.5-degree 'dog' of 4th-6th mag stars between Pleiades and Hyades; colourful stars but the figure needs imagination.

AST-EngagementRing.why: A half-degree circlet of 6th-9th mag stars with Polaris as the 'diamond'; a charming, instantly-understood view once the sky is dark.

AST-FlyingMinnow.why: A compact group of five 5th-6th mag stars (Melotte 31) shaped like a little fish near M38/IC 405; bright and pretty, shape is so-so.

AST-GolfPutter.why: A 1-degree line of stars ending in the gold double 56 Andromedae, with the large partly-resolved cluster NGC 752 as the 'ball'; a delightful field.

AST-HermansCross.why: Four ~4th-5th mag stars forming a 2-degree cross east of the Teapot; recognisable but only four stars.

AST-HomePlate.why: A pentagon of ~7th-mag stars west of M31; recognisable but faint and plain.

AST-Hyades.why: A huge V of bright stars with orange Aldebaran and many golden-orange giants and wide doubles (Theta Tauri) - a binocular showpiece that fills the field.

AST-JobsCoffin.why: The compact diamond of Delphinus' four brightest stars fits neatly in one field, with blue-white Alpha; neat but just a few bright stars.

AST-KemblesCascade.why: A 2.5-degree straight chain of ~20 faint stars with a 5th-mag star mid-way, ending in the small cluster NGC 1502: a lovely 'waterfall into a pool'.

AST-KemblesKite.why: A 2-degree diamond 'kite' with a tail of ~10 brighter stars in a bland region; pleasant and clearly shaped but low-key.

AST-LambdaLambda.why: Meissa (Lambda Ori) heads a small lambda-shaped grouping of the Collinder 69 cluster; a nice compact bright group but the shape needs some work.

AST-LittleCassiopeia.why: Lacerta's faint zig-zag W of 4th-5th magnitude stars, a few degrees long; sweep along it for a recognisable but plain pattern.

AST-Lucky7.why: A large, distinct figure '7' of brighter stars by Cassiopeia's W near M52, set in the Milky Way.

AST-NorthernFly.why: A small, sparse triangle of 4th-6th mag stars in Aries (the old constellation Musca Borealis); historical interest more than visual reward.

AST-OrionBelt.why: Three brilliant blue-white supergiants threaded by an S-shaped chain of fainter stars (Collinder 70) that fills the binocular field.

AST-Pakan3.why: A half-degree '3' (or 'M') of 8.5-9.5 mag stars; needs 15x or more and is faint.

AST-QuestionMark.why: An unmistakable 2-degree question mark of 5th-7th mag stars with Nu Ceti as the dot; clear shape, few stars.

AST-SinOrion.why: A long S-shaped chain of 15+ stars snaking between Mintaka and Alnilam within the rich Collinder 70 belt field; a lovely sight.

AST-SmileyFace.why: A 1.5-degree grin of stars just SW of M38, with Stock 8 inside; fun once seen and in a rich Auriga field.

Cr463.why: A large 6th-mag scattering of about 40 stars in northern Cassiopeia, framed nicely in a binocular field.

DS-100Her.why: A matched white 14" pair; needs 20x or so on a mount, otherwise a single star.

DS-14Ari.why: A coarse triple near Hamal; the faint 8th-mag companions are an easy but modest binocular split.

DS-15Mon.why: The close double is beyond binoculars, but the bright star crowns the Christmas Tree Cluster (NGC 2264), giving a pleasant field.

DS-16Dra.why: A wide, nearly equal white pair (90") that splits easily; pleasant but unremarkable.

DS-39Dra.why: A 5th-mag white star with a wide 8th-mag companion; the close A-B pair needs a telescope, so binoculars show only a modest unequal pair.

DS-56And.why: A wide matched orange pair right beside open cluster NGC 752, making a pretty combined binocular field.

DS-61Cyg.why: Two matched orange dwarfs 31" apart, split in steady 10x binoculars; historic as the first star with a measured distance.

DS-Albireo.why: Gold and blue stars 34" apart; steady 10x binoculars just split it and the colour contrast is a summer highlight.

DS-AlmaakDS.why: A lovely gold-and-blue double in a telescope, but at ~10" it stays unsplit in most binoculars, so you mostly see a bright orange star.

DS-AlpCap.why: A wide naked-eye pair of yellowish giants that looks striking in binoculars, with beta Cap nearby.

DS-AlpCVn.why: A bright white star with a 19.6" companion that needs steady 15x or more; modest in binoculars.

DS-AlpLib.why: Zubenelgenubi: a wide, easy 4' pair of bright white stars, a nice easy binocular double.

DS-BetMon.why: Herschel's showpiece triple is only 7" and 3" wide, so binoculars show a single star.

DS-DeltaCep.why: The prototype Cepheid, varying 3.5-4.4 in 5.4 days, with a 41" yellow-and-blue companion splittable in binoculars.

DS-DoubleDbl.why: The wide matched pair splits easily in binoculars beside Vega and zeta Lyr, though the famous 'double-double' needs a telescope.

DS-EtaCas.why: A gold-and-reddish 13" pair that needs about 24x minimum, so binoculars show a single yellowish star.

DS-GamAri.why: A lovely equal white pair in a telescope, but at 7.5" it does not split in binoculars.

DS-IotaCas.why: A fine telescopic triple, but at 2.5" and 7" it is just a single star in binoculars.

DS-MizarAlcor.why: The famous Horse and Rider: an easy wide pair in any binoculars, with Sidus Ludoviciana making a triangle; Mizar itself splits in 20x.

DS-NuDra.why: One of the finest equal-brightness binocular doubles: two identical white stars about a minute apart, the 'Dragon's eyes'.

DS-NuGem.why: A 4th-mag star with an 8th-mag companion 2' away in a rich field near M35; an easy binocular split.

DS-OmCep.why: A 3" telescopic double; just a single 5th-mag star in binoculars.

DS-OmSgr.why: A plain mag 4.7 yellow star in the faint Terebellum quadrilateral; its companion is a spectroscopic binary, not visible.

DS-PsiDra.why: A 30" pair of 4.6 and 5.6 mag stars that splits in steady binoculars; a tidy, satisfying binocular double.

DS-SigCas.why: A 3" telescopic double; unsplit and unremarkable in binoculars.

DS-ThetaTau.why: A bright wide pair (orange giant and white star) in the heart of the Hyades, so it comes with a spectacular cluster field.

DS-Winnecke4.why: M40 is just two unrelated 10th-mag stars 52" apart; a faint, underwhelming pair in binoculars.

IC2391.why: A large, bright, loose cluster of several naked-eye stars around Omicron Velorum, ideally framed by binoculars.

IC2395.why: A modest compact group in Vela, well seen in binoculars but small; forms a triangle with IC 2391 and NGC 2547.

IC2602.why: A dazzling, large group of bright blue-white stars around Theta Carinae that looks better in binoculars than in any telescope.

IC405.why: AE Aurigae is an easy star, but the nebula is at best a faint compact haze in binoculars from dark skies; the flame is photographic.

IC4651.why: A modest 10-arcminute knot near Alpha Arae, noticeable in small binoculars.

IC4665.why: A big, loose scatter of ~30 6th-8th mag stars near Beta Oph that fully resolves even in small binoculars (the 'Summer Beehive').

IC4756.why: A large, bright, richly scattered cluster that pairs with NGC 6633 for a fine binocular 'double cluster'.

LMC.why: A whole galaxy overflowing the binocular field, crowded with clusters and nebulae, with the Tarantula blazing as a bright knot.

M1.why: A small, faint oval glow that takes averted vision to see; satisfying to find but not much to look at.

M10.why: A small fuzzy disc with a visible core, best enjoyed with its twin M12 in the same field.

M100.why: The brightest of the Coma trio, a soft round glow but still a faint smudge in binoculars.

M101.why: Large but very low surface brightness; a big featureless dim patch only under very dark skies, invisible otherwise.

M102.why: The Spindle (NGC 5866) is a small, faint sliver, very difficult in binoculars.

M103.why: A small fan-shaped knot near Ruchbah, easy and pretty in a Cassiopeia field rich with other clusters.

M104.why: A tiny oval glow, made more fun by the nearby 'Stargate' triangle-in-triangle asterism and Jaws.

M105.why: A small round elliptical in the Leo trio; a faint star-like smudge.

M106.why: A faint oval spot in 10x50s on a good night; elongation hinted in larger binoculars.

M107.why: A loose, faint globular; a challenging small fuzzy spot in binoculars.

M108.why: A 10th-mag edge-on sliver; a very tough object even for the largest binoculars.

M109.why: A dim, diffuse 10th-mag galaxy lost in Phecda's glare; essentially a non-target for binoculars.

M11.why: A compact, bright mist with a brighter centre set in the Scutum star cloud; looks almost like a globular.

M110.why: M31's larger, low-surface-brightness companion; needs averted vision and a dark sky, AL rates it not visible in 7x50.

M12.why: A soft, less condensed glow; the main appeal is seeing it with M10 in one field.

M13.why: The brightest northern globular: an obvious bright ball with a defined centre, though unresolved.

M14.why: A small, faint fuzzy star with nothing to set it off.

M15.why: An easy, strongly concentrated fuzzy star beside a small triangle of stars.

M16.why: A grainy little cluster over a faint triangular nebular glow in a rich field; nebula needs dark skies.

M17.why: A distinct bright bar of nebula, sometimes with a hook, one of the few nebulae with a shape in binoculars.

M18.why: A small, dim knot of a few stars in a busy Milky Way field, easy to overlook.

M19.why: A small, faint fuzzy star; the neat line of nearby doubles is the main interest.

M2.why: A bright, round fuzzy ball with a condensed centre, but no stars resolve and the field is plain.

M20.why: A faint round glow just north of M8; its dark lanes generally need bigger binoculars.

M21.why: A compact misty cluster with a few stars showing, a bonus in the M8/M20 field.

M22.why: A big, bright globular with a broad core above the Teapot lid, the easiest globular in binoculars.

M23.why: A large, finely grained cluster about the size of the Moon with a few stars showing.

M24.why: A huge, glittering patch of Milky Way packed with hundreds of stars in striking patterns.

M25.why: A bright, loose cluster with a handful of resolved stars, plus the variable U Sgr to follow.

M26.why: A small, faint knot that barely stands out from the Scutum Milky Way.

M27.why: A surprisingly obvious small glow with a rectangular shape; the brightest planetary for binoculars.

M28.why: A small, compact globular near the Teapot lid, visible but unspectacular.

M29.why: A tiny rectangle of a few stars in the rich field near Sadr; pleasant but small.

M3.why: One of the brighter globulars: an obvious round glow with a strong core in a fairly empty field.

M30.why: A small, slightly elongated glow beside a star; easy to find but plain.

M31.why: A long glowing oval several degrees across with a bright core and companions, the showpiece galaxy in dark skies.

M32.why: A small fuzzy 'star' just off M31's disc; mainly of interest as M31's companion.

M33.why: Large but very faint, low-contrast glow that needs a dark sky; binoculars beat telescopes for it.

M34.why: A Moon-sized cluster with its brightest stars resolved over a soft glow; a pleasant easy target.

M35.why: A large, rich cluster that shows a dozen stars over haze plus a curving star string; better in larger binoculars.

M36.why: A compact, partly resolved cluster, part of the attractive Auriga trio in one sweep.

M37.why: The richest Auriga cluster, but in 10x50 a large hazy, almost nebula-like patch.

M38.why: A large, misty, loose cluster near the 'Cheshire Cat', with a few stars just resolvable.

M39.why: A big, loose triangle of fairly bright stars in Cygnus; fully resolved but sparse.

M4.why: A large, soft glow right beside brilliant Antares; a nice pairing even though the cluster stays unresolved.

M40.why: A faint, close double star that is hard to split in 10x50s; a curiosity only.

M41.why: A large, bright cluster below Sirius with many resolved stars over a glow.

M42.why: A large, bright, fan-shaped nebula with the Trapezium region and Orion's sword stars; the best nebula in binoculars.

M43.why: A small comma of glow just north of M42; part of the M42 view but hard to pick out on its own.

M44.why: A big, bright swarm of dozens of stars filling the field; a sure thing even in poor skies.

M45.why: Brilliant blue-white stars that fill the field; the binocular view rivals photographs.

M46.why: A rich but faint cluster that looks like a mottled glow, nice beside M47.

M47.why: A bright, well-resolved cluster with a chain of stars, sharing the field with misty M46.

M48.why: A large, grainy cluster like a smaller, fainter Beehive.

M49.why: A dim, featureless galaxy smudge in Virgo.

M5.why: A bright, compact globular with a strong core, easy even from town, but stays an unresolved ball.

M50.why: A moderately bright patch with a few stars resolved over haze.

M51.why: A faint, slightly elongated smudge in dark skies; the spiral arms are invisible in binoculars.

M52.why: A soft, mostly unresolved kidney-shaped glow with a yellow star at its edge.

M53.why: A faint, slightly fuzzy spot near Alpha Comae.

M54.why: A small, faint fuzzy star easy to overlook in the Teapot.

M55.why: A large, loose, low-surface-brightness globular glow low in the south.

M56.why: A faint fuzzy star between Albireo and Sulafat.

M57.why: Star-like at binocular power; the ring is not visible.

M58.why: A tiny, faint Virgo galaxy haze, a large-binocular target only.

M59.why: A faint soft patch near M60 needing dark skies and larger binoculars.

M6.why: A bright, well-resolved cluster whose stars trace butterfly wings, in a rich Milky Way field.

M60.why: A slightly easier Virgo elliptical, still a featureless patch.

M61.why: A faint galaxy patch in a starry field.

M62.why: A faint small fuzzy ball low in Ophiuchus.

M63.why: A subtle, elongated glow; at best an out-of-focus star.

M64.why: A faint oval patch on dark nights; the dark lane is invisible.

M65.why: A faint patch forming a pair with M66 in one field.

M66.why: The brighter of the Leo pair, an elongated glow beside M65.

M67.why: A soft elongated glow with a few stars resolved; rich but faint for binoculars.

M68.why: A small, unresolved spot low in Hydra.

M69.why: A small, faint star-like glow near the Teapot base.

M7.why: A huge, brilliant scatter of bright stars that just fits the binocular field, a summer highlight.

M70.why: A faint star-like point, harder than its neighbour M69.

M71.why: A dim, fairly large patch that hides in the Milky Way in Sagitta.

M72.why: A very faint, tiny globular that even large binoculars struggle with.

M73.why: An unremarkable group of four faint stars, near-stellar in binoculars.

M74.why: A very faint face-on spiral; among the hardest Messiers in binoculars.

M76.why: A tiny, faint haze, one of the hardest Messier objects in binoculars.

M77.why: A compact Seyfert galaxy that looks almost star-like in binoculars, easy to mistake for a star or tiny globular.

M78.why: A small, comet-like haze near Orion's Belt; visible in 10x50s from a dark site but with no structure.

M79.why: A small fuzzy ball low in Lepus; findable but unresolved and rated 'tougher' in 7x50s.

M8.why: A big glowing cloud with an embedded cluster and a dark lane, sharing the field with M20 and M21 under dark skies.

M80.why: A compact, bright-centred fuzzy ball between Antares and Graffias in a pleasant star field; no resolution.

M81.why: A bright oval glow with a brighter core, shared in one field with M82; one of the best galaxy views in binoculars.

M82.why: A thin elongated sliver beside M81; fainter than its partner but the pair together is a classic binocular sight.

M83.why: A fairly bright patch with a brighter core, easy from southern/dark sites but low and washed out from mid-northern latitudes.

M84.why: One of a pair of round ellipticals at the head of Markarian's Chain; two small faint 'tailless comets' in 10x50s.

M85.why: A faint featureless ball of fuzz in Coma; challenging in 50mm binoculars.

M86.why: M84's slightly larger twin; together they make a matched pair of faint glows in the Virgo field.

M87.why: One of the easier Virgo galaxies: a small round smudge, notable mainly for what it is rather than what you see.

M88.why: A faint elongated haze in Coma/Virgo, glimpsed in binoculars under dark skies only.

M89.why: A small round elliptical; just a faint star-like smudge in binoculars.

M9.why: A small, faint, star-like fuzz that is easy to miss in the Milky Way.

M90.why: A faint, low-surface-brightness oval; a challenge in small apertures.

M91.why: One of the faintest Messiers; at best a barely seen hazy patch in binoculars.

M92.why: A bright, compact globular with a strong core, easy in binoculars though overshadowed by nearby M13.

M93.why: A bright, compact arrowhead-shaped cluster partly resolved in binoculars, set in a rich Puppis Milky Way field (low from the north).

M94.why: A small, bright-cored glow, easy to see but tiny and featureless in binoculars.

M95.why: The faintest of Leo's M95/M96/M105 trio; a barely seen smudge that drops out under marginal skies.

M96.why: The brightest of the Leo trio; a faint smudge, with the reward mostly in catching all three together.

M97.why: A dim round glow needing large binoculars and averted vision; no owl 'eyes' at binocular power.

M98.why: An edge-on Coma galaxy dimmer than M100; barely detectable in binoculars.

M99.why: A round, condensed haze next to a 6th-mag star in 15x70s; low surface brightness.

Mark6.why: Just a short fuzzy arc of four 8th-9th mag stars; pleasant but minor.

Mel111.why: A huge wedge of bright stars that only binoculars can frame; the haze dissolves into many points even in small glasses.

Mel15.why: A sparse arrowhead of stars at the heart of IC 1805; the Heart Nebula itself is very hard in binoculars.

Mel20.why: Dozens of blue-white 'diamonds' scattered around yellow Mirfak; many observers rank it the best binocular cluster of the north.

NGC104.why: The second-brightest globular: a bright, nearly star-like core in a soft pearly halo, beautiful at any aperture.

NGC129.why: A sparse group showing a small triangle of 8th-9th mag stars over a dim glow between Caph and Gamma Cas.

NGC1342.why: A 6.7-mag cluster that binoculars resolve into a dozen or so stars in a mini-Scorpius shape.

NGC1502.why: A small triangular knot that is not spectacular on its own, but works as the 'splash' at the end of Kemble's Cascade in the same field.

NGC1528.why: A bright, partly resolved cluster that pairs nicely with NGC 1545 in the same Perseus field.

NGC1582.why: Big and sparse; in 7x50s only a faint wisp that blends into the background.

NGC1647.why: A large faint blur near the Hyades with an orange double at its edge; mostly unresolved in 50mm glasses.

NGC1662.why: A loose, sparse group whose ship-shaped pattern is fun once known, but it is a modest sight in binoculars.

NGC1746.why: A widely scattered field with two knots (NGC 1750/1758) between the Bull's horns; several stars visible.

NGC1807.why: A small cluster seen together with NGC 1817 as a dim 'bow tie' pair; giants binoculars needed for a cruciform.

NGC1817.why: A faint glow beside NGC 1807; its 10th-mag stars stay unresolved in most binoculars.

NGC1851.why: The brightest object in Columba: a small, concentrated globular that shows as a fuzzy ball with a bright core.

NGC1893.why: A small, faint cluster in 10x50s; the Tadpole Nebula around it is not visible.

NGC1907.why: A small, faint compact knot just south of M38; mainly interesting as M38's companion.

NGC1981.why: A bright, loose group with a line of 6th-mag stars at the top of Orion's Sword, part of a spectacular field.

NGC2158.why: A very faint, disputed smudge on M35's edge; many observers can't confirm it in binoculars.

NGC2169.why: A tiny 6' cluster; its famous '37' shape needs ~50x, so binoculars show just a small knot of stars.

NGC2232.why: A big, bright, loose cluster around blue-white 10 Mon that shows streams and a wedge of stars even in binoculars.

NGC2237.why: The central cluster NGC 2244 is easy and pretty, while the large ring of nebulosity is only a faint haze from dark skies.

NGC2244.why: A bright rectangle of 6th-7th mag stars; under dark skies the faint Rosette nebula ring may be glimpsed around it, especially with a filter.

NGC2251.why: A small 7th-mag splotch between the Rosette and Cone regions.

NGC2264.why: A bright inverted 'tree' of stars topped by 4.6-mag S Monocerotis; clearly shaped in binoculars, though the Cone Nebula is invisible.

NGC2281.why: A compact, fairly bright triangular knot of stars in eastern Auriga, a pleasant but minor binocular cluster.

NGC2301.why: A small cluster that is little more than a smudge in 50mm binoculars, though stars start to pop in stabilized 15x70s.

NGC2343.why: An easy small V of stars ('Little Hyades') paired with NGC 2335 below M50.

NGC2360.why: An easy, fairly rich glow near Sirius with its brightest stars just resolvable.

NGC2362.why: A tight sparkle of a dozen stars clinging to bright Tau CMa; a small but pretty contrast of one bright star in a glowing knot.

NGC2392.why: At binocular power it is just a faint 9th-magnitude star-like point near Wasat.

NGC2403.why: A bright non-Messier galaxy but only a faint oval glow in binoculars under good skies.

NGC2451.why: A broad, bright cluster around the orange star c Puppis, sharing the field with the rich NGC 2477; better in binoculars than a telescope.

NGC2477.why: A rich, globular-like round glow that sparkles and hints at resolution, with loose NGC 2451 in the same field.

NGC2516.why: A bright naked-eye cluster that resolves into about a hundred stars in binoculars, the south's answer to M44.

NGC2527.why: A fairly large haze in 50mm binoculars with no stars held by direct vision.

NGC253.why: One of the easiest galaxies after M31: a large, obviously elongated glow in binoculars, though without detail.

NGC2539.why: A challenging glow nearly swamped by the glare of 4th-mag 19 Puppis.

NGC2546.why: A large, irregular double cluster near zeta Puppis whose brighter members resolve in 10x50s.

NGC2547.why: A bright, loose mag-4.7 cluster of young blue stars in Vela that resolves well and sits near IC 2391.

NGC2571.why: Usually a telescopic target; 15x70s show a faint linear group of stars.

NGC2808.why: A very rich but compact globular; binoculars show only a bright, concentrated fuzzy point.

NGC2910.why: A small 5-arcminute mag-7 cluster in Vela with few bright members; little more than a faint knot.

NGC3114.why: A big, bright mag-4 cluster in Carina showing dozens of stars spread across a rich Milky Way field.

NGC3201.why: A large but loose, low-surface-brightness globular in Vela that binoculars show only dimly.

NGC3228.why: A small but bright knot of about nine 8-10 mag stars, easy in binoculars under dark sky.

NGC3242.why: Bright for a planetary but star-like in 10x50s; keen-eyed users of 70mm binoculars may catch a hint of colour.

NGC3293.why: The 'Gem Cluster': a tight, sparkling knot of bright stars next to the Eta Carinae Nebula.

NGC3372.why: A huge, bright naked-eye nebula split by the dark Keyhole lane amid rich Milky Way clusters; rivals M42 in binoculars.

NGC3532.why: A huge, bright, richly resolved cluster that John Herschel ranked among the finest in the sky; superb at low power.

NGC362.why: A bright, compact globular at the SMC's edge; an easy fuzzy ball with a bright core, overshadowed by 47 Tuc.

NGC3766.why: The 'Pearl Cluster': a compact, bright cluster that stands out in a gorgeous Centaurus Milky Way field.

NGC4463.why: A small 7th-magnitude cluster in Musca; little more than a faint knot in binoculars.

NGC4565.why: A challenging faint thin smear in 50mm binoculars; it only becomes the famous needle in larger telescopes.

NGC457.why: At binocular power the ET/Owl shows as a small bright group with Phi Cas as an 'eye'; the figure really needs a telescope.

NGC4609.why: A faint small glow beside a bright star, interesting mainly because it sits inside the dark Coalsack.

NGC4755.why: A compact, sparkling cluster next to Beta Crucis with an orange star among blue ones; lovely but small at binocular power.

NGC5128.why: A bright round glow for a galaxy, with the famous dust lane hinted in larger binoculars from dark skies.

NGC5139.why: The grandest globular: a big, bright, grainy ball that outshines M13 and M4 in binoculars when well placed.

NGC5316.why: A fairly faint, moderately large, unresolved patch near Beta Centauri.

NGC5460.why: A large, loose mag-5.6 cluster made of little groups with a neat curve of six stars.

NGC5617.why: A medium-sized bright cluster paired with Trumpler 22 just west of Alpha Centauri.

NGC5662.why: A bright, loose mag-5.5 cluster easy in small binoculars in the Centaurus Milky Way.

NGC5822.why: A large, rich star cloud in Lupus that is easy in small binoculars and best at low power.

NGC6025.why: A bright, compact V-shaped cluster with a few resolved stars over a hazy Milky Way glow.

NGC6067.why: A very rich cluster but of faint stars; shows as a grainy glow set in the bright Norma star cloud.

NGC6087.why: A blurry patch with a handful of stars, enlivened by the orange Cepheid S Normae at its heart.

NGC6124.why: A large mag-6 cluster in Scorpius that floats on a dense carpet of Milky Way stars.

NGC6134.why: A small mag-7 cluster of 12th-14th mag stars; only a faint smudge in binoculars.

NGC6167.why: A mag-6.7 cluster on the Norma-Ara border that is described as a modest-telescope object.

NGC6208.why: An old, fairly large mag-7 cluster in Ara; probably a faint grainy patch, no binocular reports found.

NGC6231.why: A compact, brilliant knot of hot blue-white stars beside the Zeta Scorpii pair at the head of the 'False Comet' - the 'Northern Jewel Box'.

NGC6397.why: One of the nearest globulars: large and bright, an easy binocular target even from mediocre skies, similar in reward to M4.

NGC6520.why: A small cluster set in the brilliant Sagittarius star cloud, with the dark Ink Spot beside it under dark skies.

NGC6530.why: The cluster embedded in the Lagoon Nebula: a sprinkle of stars set in the bright eastern glow of M8, one of the few nebulae obvious in binoculars.

NGC6541.why: A bright, concentrated globular that shows as a small hazy glow just beyond naked-eye visibility.

NGC6543.why: Spotable in binoculars thanks to high surface brightness, but only as a star-like point in a barren field.

NGC663.why: A fairly bright, rich little cluster near M103 that looks like a small round comet or horseshoe, nicer than M103 but not a showpiece.

NGC6633.why: A large, bright, loose cluster of ~30 stars that resolves well in 10x50, near the similar IC 4756 - a fine pair-of-clusters field.

NGC6709.why: A moderately rich but faint (mag 6.7, stars 9th-11th) cluster in the Aquila Milky Way; a small grainy patch in binoculars.

NGC6716.why: A loose, poorly concentrated 7th-mag cluster with no notable binocular reports.

NGC6752.why: The fourth-brightest globular, a puffy almost-stellar core in a halo three-quarters the Moon's size.

NGC6802.why: A tiny dim mist at the end of the Coathanger bar; only of interest as a bonus beside the asterism.

NGC6819.why: A rich but compact glow in the Cygnus Milky Way; the stars stay unresolved in typical binoculars.

NGC6823.why: A small compact cluster in the Vulpecula Milky Way; its nebula is too faint for binoculars.

NGC6826.why: In 50mm binoculars it is just a dim star; the famous blinking needs a telescope.

NGC6871.why: A bright group of 5th-7th mag stars set in the rich Cygnus Milky Way, with a neat triangle core.

NGC6885.why: A small group around the bright star 20 Vulpeculae that is easily missed in the star's glare; some call it a binocular treat but it is modest.

NGC6888.why: Too faint for binoculars without a filter; observers recommend 4-8 inch telescopes with OIII to see the crescent.

NGC6910.why: A compact knot with two 7th-mag 'feet' half a degree from Sadr; easy but small and mostly unresolved.

NGC6934.why: A difficult, star-like 9th-mag smudge in dark skies only.

NGC6940.why: A rich, large cluster in the Vulpecula Milky Way that is partly resolved in binoculars but blends into the background star field.

NGC6960.why: A thin filament running through bright 52 Cygni; findable in 7x50s under dark skies but faint and fighting the star's glare.

NGC6992.why: Under a dark sky its brightest arc shows as a long curving hazy streak, a thrill to see unaided by a filter, much better with OIII.

NGC7000.why: A huge nebula that is better in binoculars than telescopes; under a dark sky the 'Gulf of Mexico' dark lane and Florida/Mexico shapes show, but it needs dark skies.

NGC7009.why: A tiny 8th-magnitude planetary that looks like a slightly defocused star even at 15x70.

NGC7063.why: A small, scattered mag-7 group in Cygnus; only a few stars show and it is easily lost in the rich field.

NGC7160.why: A bright little knot in Cepheus: a blue mag-7 star and two others make a tiny triangle over a faint glow.

NGC7209.why: A hazy patch with a handful of pinpoint stars in Lacerta, a magnitude fainter than nearby NGC 7243.

NGC7235.why: A small, sparse, distant mag-7.7 cluster near zeta Cephei; at best a faint little patch in binoculars.

NGC7243.why: A coarse, irregular half-degree cluster in Lacerta; binoculars show a handful of 8th-9th mag stars over a hazy background.

NGC7293.why: Large but very low surface brightness; binoculars show only a round hazy smudge from a dark, moonless site.

NGC7331.why: A faint elongated glow that needs dark skies and at least 10x50s; satisfying to catch but not much to look at.

NGC752.why: A large, loose cluster nearly a degree across, partially resolved into chains of faint stars, with the bright orange/gold pair 56 And beside it.

NGC7662.why: Reachable in 50mm binoculars but it looks like a star; the blue disc needs a telescope.

NGC7789.why: A rich but faint cluster (brightest stars ~11th mag) that appears in binoculars as a round, grainy, unresolved glow.

NGC869.why: Two rich, sparkling clusters side by side in one binocular field, with scattered red supergiants - a top-tier binocular showpiece.

NGC884.why: Two rich, sparkling clusters side by side in one binocular field, with scattered red supergiants - a top-tier binocular showpiece.

NGC891.why: A very low surface brightness edge-on streak; barely detectable in binoculars with a tripod and averted vision.

SMC.why: A naked-eye galaxy that fits a binocular field, studded with clusters and nebulae and flanked by 47 Tuc and NGC 362.

STAR-Aldebaran.why: A bright orange giant whose colour stands out against the white Hyades stars in the same binocular field.

STAR-Algol.why: The classic eclipsing binary: you can watch it fade from mag 2.1 to 3.4 over a few hours against nearby comparison stars.

STAR-Alphard.why: An orange giant whose colour binoculars bring out, alone in a blank patch of sky.

STAR-Antares.why: A fiery red supergiant that shares the binocular field with globular M4 in rich Scorpius star fields.

STAR-Arcturus.why: A dazzling golden-orange star; binoculars (slightly defocused) bring out its colour, but it is a lone star.

STAR-Betelgeuse.why: A brilliant, obviously orange-red supergiant whose colour pops in binoculars, especially against blue Rigel and Bellatrix.

STAR-Capella.why: A brilliant star with a distinct yellow tinge; pleasant in binoculars but just a single point.

STAR-Deneb.why: A bright white star set in the rich Cygnus Milky Way, with the North America Nebula half a field away.

STAR-Fomalhaut.why: A bright white star alone in an empty sky region; nothing much to see beyond the point itself.

STAR-LaSuperba.why: A variable carbon star whose deep orange-red colour shows strongly in binoculars, often called the finest binocular carbon star.

STAR-Mira.why: Near maximum a strikingly red-orange star whose brightness changes enormously over months; invisible in binoculars at its faintest.

STAR-MuCep.why: One of the reddest naked-eye stars; in binoculars, next to white Alderamin, its deep garnet colour is immediately obvious.

STAR-Procyon.why: A bright yellow-white star with nothing special to show in binoculars.

STAR-Rasalgethi.why: A prominently orange, slowly varying red giant; the famous colourful companion is too close to split in binoculars.

STAR-Sirius.why: The brightest star; when low, binoculars show it flashing through rainbow colours.

STAR-Vega.why: A dazzling blue-white star; attractive, and epsilon Lyrae's wide pair is nearby, but itself just a point.

Stock2.why: A big grainy stick-figure ('Muscleman') of 8th-9th mag stars that stands out well near the Double Cluster.

Stock23.why: About six stars standing out nicely in a trapezoid like a tiny Draco's head.

Tr2.why: A loose 6th-mag cluster near the Double Cluster; nicer in binoculars than by eye, but modest.

Tr3.why: A hazy, low-contrast grouping of a few faint bluish stars with a pretty arc nearby.
